Q: How do you test Lua code in an Istio EnvoyFilter resource via K3S TestContainers? A:

Got a working solution which I thought I would share, feel free to comment and suggest improvements. So I added the TestContainers K3S Module to Gradle and created a Java test as follows:

import lombok.extern.slf4j.Slf4j;
import org.testcontainers.k3s.K3sContainer;
import org.testcontainers.utility.DockerImageName;
import org.testcontainers.utility.MountableFile;

@Slf4j // lombok to add a logger
public class K3sIstioTest {

    private static final int K3S_PORT = 6443, NGINX_PORT = 30080;
    private static final DockerImageName k3sImage = DockerImageName.parse("k3s-istio:latest")
            .asCompatibleSubstituteFor("rancher/k3s");
    private static final K3sContainer k3s = new K3sContainer(k3sImage)
            .withReuse(true)
            .withCopyFileToContainer(
                    MountableFile.forClasspathResource("kubernetes"),
                    "/kubernetes"
            )
            .withAccessToHost(true)
            .withExposedPorts(K3S_PORT, NGINX_PORT);

}

This creats a K3sContainer instance with a custom Docker image, mounts src/test/resources/kubernetes Java folder to /kubernetes on the running container and exposes the K3S port and Nginx (our sample K3S app).

The bespoke Docker image k3s-istio is as follows:

Dockerfile

# Stage 1: Download curl / istioctl binary
FROM alpine:3.18 as alphine-downloader
RUN apk add --no-cache curl tar jq
RUN curl -L https://github.com/istio/istio/releases/latest/download/istioctl-1.28.3-linux-amd64.tar.gz | \
    tar xz -C /tmp istioctl

# Final stage: Use official k3s image and add istioctl
FROM rancher/k3s:v1.35.0-k3s1

# Copy istioctl from downloader stage
COPY --from=alphine-downloader /tmp/istioctl /usr/local/bin/istioctl
RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/istioctl

# Set KUBECONFIG environment variable so that K3S kubectl works out of the box
ENV KUBECONFIG=/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml

# Add uesful aliases 
RUN mkdir -p /etc/profile.d && \
    echo "alias k=kubectl" > /etc/profile.d/aliases.sh && \
    echo "alias i=istioctl" >> /etc/profile.d/aliases.sh && \
    echo "alias l='ls -al'" >> /etc/profile.d/aliases.sh && \
    echo "kn() { kubectl get ns ; echo ; if [ \"\$#\" -eq 1 ]; then kubectl config set-context --current --namespace \$1 ; echo ; fi ; echo \"Current namespace [ \$(kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace | cut -d ' ' -f6) ]\" ; }" >> /etc/profile.d/aliases.sh 

# Make aliases available in shells
ENV ENV=/etc/profile.d/aliases.sh

This Dockerfile is a multi-stage build where the first stage adds curl and istioctl to an Alpine base image. The final stage is to use the official K3S image and add istioctl from the first stage.

NOTE: The reason we're using a multi-stage build is that K3S image doesn't have apk or curl installed which makes installing istioctl very tricky.

To build run:

docker build . -t k3s-istio

The next stage is to add a @BeforeAll section to the K3sIstioTest class:

    @BeforeAll
    public static void beforeAll() throws Exception {
        k3s.start();

        log.info("Installing Istio");
        k3sExec("istioctl install --set profile=default -y");
        kubectlWaitAllPodsReady(120);
        log.info("Istio installation complete");

        // Nginx
        log.info("Installing Nginx");
        kubectl("apply -f kubernetes/nginx.yml -n nginx");
    }

Installing Istio on K3S cluster is now as simple as running istioctl install --set profile=default -y. You may notice 3 methods:

  1. k3sExec - execute any command in K3S container and throws exception if it fails.
  2. kubectl - runs kubectl commands in K3S e.g. apply -f kubernetes/nginx.yml -n nginx.
  3. kubectlWaitAllPodsReady - wait until all K3S pods in all namespaces are "ready".

These methods are:

    private static void k3sExec(String command, Object... params) throws Exception {
        String cmd = String.format(command, params);
        Container.ExecResult result = k3s.execInContainer("sh", "-c", cmd);
        if (result.getExitCode() != 0) {
            String errorMessage = String.format(
                    "Failed with code %d: %s\nOutput: %s\nError: %s",
                    result.getExitCode(),
                    cmd,
                    result.getStdout(),
                    result.getStderr()
            );
            throw new RuntimeException(errorMessage);
        }
    }

    private static void kubectl(String kubectlCommand, Object... params) throws Exception {
        k3sExec("kubectl " + kubectlCommand, params);
    }

    private static void kubectlWaitAllPodsReady(int timeoutSeconds) throws Exception {
        kubectl("wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all --all-namespaces --timeout=%ds", timeoutSeconds);
    }

To install Nginx simply add a nginx.yml file into the src/test/resources/kubernetes folder:

src/test/resources/kubernetes/nginx.yml

apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    istio-injection: enabled
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-conf
data:
  default.conf: |
    map $http_x_correlation_id $correlation_id_json {
      default '';
      ~.+ ', "x-correlation-id": "$http_x_correlation_id"';
    }
    server {
      listen 80;
      server_name localhost;
      default_type application/json;
      charset utf-8;  
      location / {
        return 200 '{"message": "welcome"$correlation_id_json}';
      }
      location /health {
        return 200 '{"status": "ok"$correlation_id_json}';
      }
    }

First of all we create a nginx namespace with a label istio-injection: enabled. This ensures Istio will create a sidecar container in the nginx pod which e.g. can proxy / manipulate network traffic.

Next we create a very basic nginx-conf configmap which configures Nginx with 2 endpoints (/ and /health). This server supports an optional x-correlation-id header and insert it into the response body if it exists.

Lets add Deployment and Service resources to nginx.yml to complete the Nginx installation:

---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nginx
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: basic
          image: nginx
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: nginx-conf
              mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
              subPath: default.conf
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: nginx-conf
          configMap:
            name: nginx-conf
            items:
              - key: default.conf
                path: default.conf
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
      nodePort: 30080

The service nodePort is set to 30080 which we expose in the K3S container (NGINX_PORT).

Finally, lets add a @Test Junit method to the K3sIstioTest class which will hit the available Nginx endpoints (e.g. using REST Assured):

    @Test
    public void testNginxHome() {
        nginxRestAssured()
                .header("x-correlation-id", "1234-6789")
                .get("/")
                .then()
                .statusCode(200)
                .body("message", equalTo("welcome"),
                        "x-correlation-id", equalTo("1234-6789"));
    }

    private static RequestSpecification nginxRestAssured() {
        return RestAssured.given()
                .baseUri("http://localhost:" + k3s.getMappedPort(NGINX_PORT))
                .contentType(ContentType.JSON)
                .when();
    }

Running this method will do the following:

  1. Run our K3S container with istioctl installed.

  2. Setup Istio on K3S environment using istioctl CLI.

  3. Deploy Nginx on K3S using the nginx.yml via kubectl.

  4. Ensure all pods are healthy before ...

  5. ... hitting the / endpoint via RestAssured and asserting the body is correct.

After the test has run you can also curl the K3S container directly by running docker ps | grep k3s:

1347daf54247   k3s-istio:latest   ...   0.0.0.0:54113->30080/tcp  ....

For example we can curl on the exposed Nginx port 54113 i.e.

curl -H 'x-correlation-id: 1234' http://localhost:54113/health

Should return:

{
  "status": "ok", 
  "x-correlation-id": "1234"
}

We can also execute into the K3S container via the container id i.e. docker exec -it 1347daf54247 sh. Once inside we can look at the running pods:

~ # kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
NAMESPACE      NAME                                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
istio-system   istio-ingressgateway-6b89d47f9d-7sqtw       1/1     Running   0          5m21s
istio-system   istiod-5b4c5695cd-pw72q                     1/1     Running   0          5m35s
kube-system    coredns-54bf7cdff9-hkkzs                    1/1     Running   0          5m36s
...
nginx          nginx-7f46bc5fb5-ztdz9                      2/2     Running   0          5m1s

Notice the nginx pod has 2 containers (2/2) which shows Istio is proxying the traffic.

To prove Istio is working let's create the following:

src/test/resources/kubernetes/istio-filter.yml

---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: add-correlation-id
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels:
      app: nginx
  priority: 10
  configPatches:
    - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER
      match:
        context: SIDECAR_INBOUND
        listener:
          filterChain:
            filter:
              name: "envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager"
              subFilter:
                name: "envoy.filters.http.router"
      patch:
        operation: INSERT_BEFORE
        value:
          name: envoy.lua
          typed_config:
            "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.lua.v3.Lua
            inline_code: |
              function generate_uuid()
                local template = 'xxxxxxxx-xxxx-4xxx-yxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx'
                return string.gsub(template, '[xy]', function(c)
                  local v = (c == 'x') and math.random(0, 15) or math.random(8, 11)
                  return string.format('%x', v)
                end)
              end
              
              function envoy_on_request(request_handle)
                request_handle:logInfo("--- Lua filter executing ---")

                local correlation_id = generate_uuid()
                if request_handle:headers():get("x-correlation-id") == null then
                  request_handle:headers():add("x-correlation-id", correlation_id)
                  request_handle:logInfo("Added x-correlation-id: " .. correlation_id)
                else
                  request_handle:headers():replace("x-correlation-id", correlation_id)
                  request_handle:logInfo("Replaced x-correlation-id: " .. correlation_id)
                end 
              
                request_handle:logInfo("--- Lua filter finished ---")
              end

This will add an Istio Envoy Filter resource which will generate a UUID and then add (or replace) a x-correlation-id header with this UUID value.

Now let's update the beforeAll() to add this istio resource and also wirte code to restart the nginx pod:

    @BeforeAll
    public static void beforeAll() throws Exception {
        // existing code

        kubectl("apply -f kubernetes/istio-filter.yml -n nginx");

        kubectlWaitAllPodsReady(120);
        kubectl("rollout restart deployment nginx -n nginx");
        kubectl("rollout status deployment nginx -n nginx --timeout=60s");
    }

We also need to update our testNginxHome test method i.e.

    @Test
    public void testNginxHome() {
        nginxRestAssured()
                .header("x-correlation-id", "1234-6789")
                .get("/")
                .then()
                .statusCode(200)
                .body("message", equalTo("welcome"),
                        "x-correlation-id", matchesPattern("[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}"));
    }

NOTE: Before running this method you may need to run docker rm -f <k3s-container-id

Notice that although we are passing the header x-correlation-id: 1234-6789 we are asserting that the header matches the format of a UUID. This proves the the Enovy filter works. We can also test with a curl again:

curl -H 'x-correlation-id: 1234' http://localhost:54113

Will return:

{
  "message": "welcome", 
  "x-correlation-id": "cb9c1a5b-6910-4fb2-b457-a9c72a392d90"
}

Finally, we can check the logs directly by jumping into the K3S container (docker exec -it <k3s-container-id> sh) and running:

POD_NAME=$(kubectl get pod -n nginx -l app=nginx -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
istioctl proxy-config -n nginx log $POD_NAME --level lua:debug,filter:debug
kubectl logs -n nginx -fl app=nginx -c istio-proxy --tail=200

This sets the Istio log level using istioctl so we can see Lua execution logs.

Now if we re-run the curl again (in a different window) we should see this in the logs:

2026-01-21T10:21:30.999872Z     info    ... script log: --- Lua filter executing ---        thread=22
2026-01-21T10:21:30.999920Z     info    envoy lua external/envoy/source/extensions/filters/common/lua/lua.cc:26 script log: Replaced x-correlation-id: d0dad24e-515e-40ab-a120-7b8d24ecbad0     thread=22
2026-01-21T10:21:30.999928Z     info    envoy lua external/envoy/source/extensions/filters/common/lua/lua.cc:26 script log: --- Lua filter finished --- thread=22
2026-01-21T10:21:30.999929Z     debug   envoy lua external/envoy/source/extensions/filters/common/lua/lua.cc:67 coroutine finished      thread=22

The key log is:

  • Replaced x-correlation-id: d0dad24e-515e-40ab-a120-7b8d24ecbad0

The UUID in the log should match the response of the curl.

Conclusion

This proves we can integration test Istio via K3S / test containers which is really powerful for testing things like Lua code inside Istio EnvoyFilter resources but we could test other things like JWT validation, authorization policies etc.

Also, Nginx can be replaced for any target application which matches your use case and the Dockerfile could be extend to support e.g. Helm which help integration test various Kubernetes scenarios without having to deploy to a live environment.

Q: Does V8 optimize curried functions like a typical functional programming language? A:

Also because JavaScript is not a lazy evaluation language, the term "currying" does not really apply. There's no real difference between a function that happens to reference a symbol from an enclosing lexical scope and one that doesn't, in terms of how the code runs.

Q: Networkx with errors from adding nodes and edges A:

The format expected by add_edges_from is a list of tuples, in its most basic form, as a list of (u,v) pairs to connect.

Your files don't have the data in an appropriate form so networkx doesn't know what to do with them. If the text is exactly as you wrote in the "edges" variable, then below is one way to massage it into the right kind of list. You can do similar for the node processing, though this only needs a list of elements, not a list of tuples so is more straightforward.

with open("edgefile.txt") as data_file:
    data_edges = data_file.read()

# split on the comma, assuming this divides elements, remove the curly braces and quotes
elems = ([f.strip(" {}'") for f in data_edges.strip().split(',')])
# use zip to turn the flat list into a lst of pairs
edge_list = zip(elems[::2], elems[1::2])

# now we are in a form that nx.add_edges_from can handle
G = nx.Graph()
G.add_nodes_from(nodes)
G.add_edges_from(edge_list)

You should read the docs on reading in graphs here: https://networkx.github.io/documentation/stable/reference/readwrite/index.html

which describes how to read from various standard graph formats.

EDIT following qu in comment:

The reason that you have many "unexpected" nodes in the graph is because nx.add_nodes_from takes an iterable type, and when you read the whole file into a text variable, iterating over that string takes one character at at time. This produces the single-character nodes like 0, ', and \n. So we can fix it by parsing the string into a list, and iterating over a list gives one element, like '0000000002'.

Here is an example:

# assume that the file describing nodes is read into this string:
node_txt = "'0000000002', '0000000101', '0000000111', '0000000200', '0000000502', '0000000600', '0000001000', '0000001001', '0000001069', '0000001253', '0000001462', '0000003013', '0000003200', '0000004100', '0000004305', '0000005100', '0000005460', '0000006600', '0000010021', '0000010101', '0000010200', '0000010314', '0000012000', '0000012151', '0000012600', '0000015201', '0000016100', '0000017002', '0000020002', '0000020050', '0000020100', '0000021001', '0000022044', '0000022100'\n"

G1 = nx.Graph()
G1.add_nodes_from(node_txt)
print(G1.nodes())
print(set(node_txt))
# output of these two commands shows that the node names are 1 char each:
>>> [' ', "'", '\n', ',', '1', '0', '3', '2', '5', '4', '7', '6', '9']
>>> set([' ', "'", '\n', ',', '1', '0', '3', '2', '5', '4', '7', '6', '9'])

# reference: what we really wanted    
node_list = ['0000000002', '0000000101', '0000000111', '0000000200', '0000000502', '0000000600', '0000001000', '0000001001', '0000001069', '0000001253', '0000001462', '0000003013', '0000003200', '0000004100', '0000004305', '0000005100', '0000005460', '0000006600', '0000010021', '0000010101', '0000010200', '0000010314', '0000012000', '0000012151', '0000012600', '0000015201', '0000016100', '0000017002', '0000020002', '0000020050', '0000020100', '0000021001', '0000022044', '0000022100']

G2  = nx.Graph()
G2.add_nodes_from(node_list)
print(G2.nodes())
print(set(node_list))

So how to transform node_txt into the form of node_list? We follow the same process as described above for the edges - this one is a bit simpler.

elems = [f.strip(" '") for f in node_txt.strip().split(',')]
print(elems == node_list)
# output: True -> so here we recovered the node names correctly from node_txt
